8.3.3.2 Fauna
Although detailed information concerning fish and wildlife populations at the Coley Creek site is unavailable to the FPC Staff, it is expected that the area is similar to the Bad Creek site and supports similar wildlife species and populations. The area has been described as remote with a wildland character, and signs of bear and other wildlife have been reported throughout the site (Dysart, et al., 1973). Managed for wildlife by the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission, the land at the site is considered prime for hunting (Dysart, et al., 1973).
The Coley Creek Reservoir would inundate land now being used for wildlife habitat and for hunting opportunities. Adverse effects on wildlife species as a result of impoundment, construction, clearing activities, and operation of the project would be similar in kind, but greater in number of individuals affected than those described for the Bad Creek site in Subsections 3.1.2 and 3.2.2.
Coley Creek has been classified by the State of North Carolina as a valuable trout nursery stream, but too small to support significant fishing (Fish, 1968). About 1 mile of stream habitat would be inundated by the upper reservoir, eliminating those species dependent on a stream environment, unless they could adapt to conditions in the reservoir. Approximately 2.2 miles of stream between the dam and Lake Jocassee would be adversely affected by increased turbidity resulting from construction and clearing activities. Impacts similar to those described for the Bad Creek area would be experienced. Flow in Coley Creek could be limited to seepage from the upper reservoir and any local inflows between the dam and Lake Jocassee. Such a flow reduction would further reduce the suitability of the stream for production of trout and other fish species. Measures to augment flows in Coley Creek below the project dams could also adversely affect trout production if water with different characteristics from those of Coley Creek is utilized.
A portion of Lake Jocassee at or near its confluence with the Thompson River could experience increases in turbidity as a result of construction and clearing activities at the Coley Creek site. Such increases would be expected to last only until disturbed areas are rehabilitated by seeding of grasses, reforestation, and other measures. Should turbid conditions persist in that area, fish species might move to other portions of the lake.
